title: Data sovereignty routing design notes
body:
Purpose:
This notes doc captures design options and tradeoffs for enforcing data sovereignty constraints in customer deployments. It focuses on routing and hosting options (hosted, dedicated, private) and proposes a small set of tested patterns for customers with regulatory requirements (example customer: NordBank EU).

Context & constraints:
- Customer: mid-size European bank requiring EU-only processing for PII, audit trails, and customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM).
- Workload: low-to-medium traffic interactive chat and document summarization, 150–600 QPS burst, typical request payloads contain PII.
- SLOs: 95th-percentile latency < 350ms for short-turn queries, availability > 99.9% in primary region.
- Security: SOC2/ISO alignment, audit logs exported to customer SIEM, retention 1 year.

High-level design goals:
1) Guarantee regional processing (data residency) without doubling cost unnecessarily.
2) Maintain developer experience parity with hosted API where possible.
3) Offer clear rollback/fallback behavior when local capacity is exhausted.
4) Provide auditable key control and minimal surface area for data exfiltration.

Options considered (summary):
A. Hosted with region-pin + customer-managed logging partitioning
B. Dedicated (Redwood-managed dedicated capacity in customer region) with VPC peering and KMS integration
C. Private deployment (customer-managed control plane and inference in customer VPC or on-prem)
D. Hybrid: hosted control plane + private/dedicated data plane in EU

Detailed tradeoffs:
- Option A (Hosted regional): fastest time-to-onboard, lowest initial cost. Limitations: trust boundary (control plane outside customer control possible), potential for subtle cross-region failover unless strict routing policies enforced. Best for customers comfortable with Redwood-hosted control plane and contractual guarantees.
- Option B (Dedicated region): predictable throughput and stronger isolation; Redwood operates GPUs in region; supports KMS integration. Tradeoffs include reserved capacity cost and slower scale-up to unexpected peaks; good compromise for regulated customers wanting Redwood to operate infra but within region.
- Option C (Private): maximum control and auditability, customer owns VPC/networking and can satisfy strict data residency laws. Higher operational burden and longer lead time; may limit some Redwood-managed features (e.g., multi-tenant analytics).
- Option D (Hybrid): control plane hosted, inference data plane in customer region (dedicated pods or private connectors). Balances developer experience and data locality; needs hardened control-plane <-> data-plane auth and network policies.

Routing patterns & enforcement primitives:
1) Region pinning: include a region tag in request metadata (e.g., region=EU-1); runtime rejects or routes only to capacity with matching residency guarantees.
2) Data-plane separation: enforce that any KV cache, logs, and ephemeral model state for EU requests are hosted only on EU-located capacity.
3) Fallback policy: explicit 'no-cross-border-fallback' boolean — if true, runtime returns capacity-exhausted instead of routing to non-EU fallback.
4) Tiered-fallback: for less-sensitive flows (non-PII), allow cross-region cheap model fallback. Must be opt-in per route.

Example policy snippet (pseudocode):
- route: /api/v1/generate
  - policy: residency: EU_ONLY
  - fallback: NONE
  - key_management: customer-kms-eu-1
  - log_destination: customer-s3-eu-logs

Operational considerations:
- Autoscaling and burst: Dedicated/dedicated-hybrid must have pre-warmed burst pools in-region; private deployments should have a sizing plan and warmup scripts.
- Monitoring: require per-route telemetry exposing region tag, matched capacity id, and KMS key id.
- Audit: immutable request trace ID, signed event stream stored in customer's EU logs with checksum proof.
- SLO enforcement: circuit-breaker when EU capacity saturates (fail fast + clear error code) to avoid silent cross-border routing.

Cost & latency examples (ballpark):
- Hosted (EU region): $0.018 per token served (metering includes multi-tenant improvements). Latency: base 100–180ms.
- Dedicated (reserved): higher base (reserve + per-token) — approx 1.6x hosted cost but latency more predictable: 80–150ms p95.
- Private (on-prem): highest operational cost due to infra amortization, but can match or beat dedicated latency if hardware is local.

Suggested default recommendation matrix (for NordBank-like customer):
- If customer accepts Redwood-hosted control plane and requires EU residency but low compliance overhead: Option D (hybrid) with EU data plane + hosted control plane.
- If customer requires Redwood to operate everything inside EU and wants managed service: Option B (dedicated EU-only).
- If customer insists on owning keys, networks, and control plane: Option C (private).

Migration and rollout plan (3-phase):
Phase 0 — discovery (2 weeks): validate regulatory clauses, list required KMS/HSM vendors, confirm SIEM endpoints.
Phase 1 — pilot (4–6 weeks): small sandbox workload (non-production data) deployed to EU data plane; verify routing, tracing, KMS integration, audit exports.
Phase 2 — staged rollout (6–10 weeks): route 10% traffic -> 50% -> 100% with canary SLO gates. Maintain explicit circuit-breaker to avoid cross-border routing.

Testing & validation checklist:
- Unit tests for region-pinning middleware.
- Integration test: simulate EU capacity exhaustion and verify fallback behavior (should fail fast unless allowed).
- Penetration test for control-plane to data-plane auth tokens.
- Key-rotation drill: ensure customer KMS rotation does not break live requests.
- Audit replay: be able to reconstruct request flow from logs and prove residency.

Open questions / risks:
- SLA language must explicitly prohibit automatic cross-region failover for EU_ONLY routes; contract + product enforcement needed.
- Cost model for long tail compliance (customers with multiple residency constraints across multiple regions).
- Observable artifacts required by compliance teams (format, retention, tamper-proofing).

Next steps & action items:
- [Owner: Priya] Draft a short customer-facing one-pager summarizing the hybrid recommendation and estimated lead times (due: 2025-11-20).
- [Owner: Aiden] Prototype region-pinning middleware in staging and capture test vector (due: 2025-11-28).
- [Owner: Lucas] Run capacity-saturation test on dedicated EU cluster and report latency behavior (due: 2025-12-05).

Appendix: quick glossary
- Data plane: infrastructure that handles raw request payloads and model execution.
- Control plane: orchestration, routing policies, billing, and management features.
- Region pinning: policy asserting that a request must be processed in a specific geographic region.

End of notes.
